concept.name: Rebalancing
concept.definition: The process of bringing a portfolio back to its original or target asset allocation mix, which becomes necessary because some investments grow faster than others and push the portfolio out of alignment with its intended risk level.
concept.intuition: If your winners grow faster than your losers, your portfolio quietly becomes riskier (or safer) than you planned; rebalancing trims the winners and tops up the laggards to restore the plan.
concept.mechanics: Rebalancing can be calendar-based (e.g., every 6 or 12 months) or threshold-based (when an asset class weight moves beyond a preset band), and is executed by selling overweighted categories to buy underweighted ones, by directing new contributions to underweighted categories, or both.
concept.failure_modes: Each rebalance can trigger transaction costs and taxable gains, and in strong trending markets disciplined rebalancing systematically sells the asset that keeps rising, lagging a drifted buy-and-hold portfolio.
concept.misconceptions: Rebalancing is a risk-control discipline, not a return-boosting trick: its 'buy low, sell high' effect does not guarantee higher returns, only that the portfolio's risk stays near its target.
concept.example: An investor targets 60% stocks; after a rally stocks reach 80% of the portfolio, so she sells stocks or directs new savings into bonds until the 60/40 mix is restored.

citations.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Beginners' Guide to Asset Allocation, Diversification, and Rebalancing
